profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between two partners preparing a county-level wildfire planning support package that will use LANDFIRE layers for a multi-agency fuels prioritization workshop in western Colorado. Context: the county emergency manager has asked for a map package and brief methods summary before a workshop scheduled for the following Friday, so the team needs to decide what products to assemble, what level of local adjustment to make, who will do each piece, and when draft materials will be ready. Agenda: confirm which LANDFIRE products to include, define what 'local calibration' and 'final maps' entail, assign responsibility for preparing maps and metadata, and set an internal timeline for review. Expected outcome: a shared-seeming plan for producing the workshop package, including a draft map set, a short methods memo, and a review schedule.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Community wildfire protection planning, interagency coordination, and translating geospatial fire products for local decision-makers
members.background: Elena works for the county emergency management office and routinely assembles planning materials for fire districts, commissioners, and community groups; she is not the primary GIS producer but has enough technical familiarity to coordinate map-based planning efforts.
members.private_state: She wants a workshop-ready package that county stakeholders can immediately use without being distracted by technical caveats, and she is worried that too much complexity or too many draft labels will reduce confidence in the process.
hidden_assumptions: When partners say they will use LANDFIRE for local planning, they will minimally adjust obvious local discrepancies before anything is shown publicly.
A 'final map' for a workshop means a polished PDF map book with legends, annotations, and county-specific overlays suitable for direct presentation.
The 'Friday deadline' refers to materials being in her inbox by close of business local time so she can assemble and print packets that evening.
If someone agrees to document methods, that includes a short plain-language explanation of caveats and local edits for nontechnical county participants.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: LANDFIRE products, raster processing workflows, disturbance updates, and reproducible geospatial analysis for fuels and fire planning
members.background: Marcus supports a regional interagency fire planning office and regularly prepares standardized LANDFIRE-derived layers and technical metadata for partner agencies, with an emphasis on consistency and traceable methods across jurisdictions.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the package aligned with standard LANDFIRE-derived workflows, avoid ad hoc local edits that break reproducibility, and deliver something efficient enough to fit alongside several other partner requests this week.
hidden_assumptions: When a partner asks for LANDFIRE-based planning support, the default is to provide standardized statewide or county-clipped products unless a separate local data integration step has already been formally approved.
A 'final map' means the final set of GIS layers and exported standard layouts that are analytically complete, even if local briefing annotations are added later by the partner.
The 'Friday deadline' refers to posting deliverables by end of day on the federal shared drive, which can happen after local office hours.
Documenting methods means attaching the standard metadata and processing notes, not rewriting caveats into a public-facing narrative.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to do a 'light local calibration' before the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena believes this includes manually correcting a few obvious misclassified recent treatment areas and a known irrigated valley bottom that local chiefs always flag, so the workshop maps will reflect local reality.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus believes this means only clipping LANDFIRE layers to the county boundary and, at most, applying already-published disturbance updates already in the federal workflow, with no hand edits based on local knowledge.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see their interpretation as the obvious minimal meaning of 'light' calibration, and because neither is proposing a major methodological change, the phrase sounds safely low-stakes and does not trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to having the 'final maps' ready for Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a workshop-ready PDF packet with title pages, callouts for communities and evacuation corridors, legend explanations, and consistent page numbering for printing and discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the final analytical map outputs: county-clipped raster layers plus a few exported layouts from the standard template, with any presentation polish to be handled downstream.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In planning conversations, 'final maps' is a natural umbrella term that often bundles analysis and presentation together, so each assumes the other shares the same practical endpoint.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the package will be 'done by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena thinks 'done' means delivered to her by 5:00 PM Mountain Time Friday so she can review, combine, and print before the Monday workshop prep session.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus thinks 'done' means uploaded before midnight on Friday to the interagency SharePoint with all files present, even if Elena does not look at them until later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline shorthand like 'by Friday' is routine and usually passes without discussion, especially when both are trying to sound flexible and cooperative rather than pedantic about timing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Marcus will provide a 'methods note' to accompany the map package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena expects a one- to two-page plain-language memo summarizing what LANDFIRE layers were used, what local adjustments were made, and how county participants should interpret limitations during the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus expects to attach the standard processing log, metadata snippets, and a bullet list of layer names and versions generated from his workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A 'methods note' sounds like a minor accessory deliverable, so both treat it as straightforward housekeeping and never unpack audience, format, or level of explanation.

When I say final maps, I mean a polished PDF packet with legends, page numbers, community labels, evacuation corridors, and county overlays already baked in. And done by Friday means in my inbox by close of business Mountain Time so I can assemble the packets that evening. The methods note also needs to be plain-language enough that people trust what they're seeing.
